# Toolbar

**Status:** stable

A row or column of controls that is one tab stop, with arrow-key movement between its items (role="toolbar"), over Base UI Toolbar. Items reuse Button's ghost variants and Input, so they follow density like every other control.

**Keywords:** toolbar, action bar, button row, icon buttons, formatting bar, roving focus, arrow keys, tool chrome, editor toolbar

## Usage

Use Toolbar when three or more related controls sit together and act on the same thing — a text selection, a canvas, a document, a table. Tab lands on the toolbar once and the arrow keys move along it, so a keyboard user crosses an editor's twelve buttons in one keystroke instead of twelve. It works in both registers: ghost sm buttons on a page, compact icon-xs buttons inside a Workspace.

### Best practices

- Do: Give every Toolbar an aria-label that names what it acts on ("Text formatting", "Canvas"). With more than one toolbar on screen, that label is the only way a screen-reader user tells them apart.
- Do: Use size="icon-sm" (page) or size="icon-xs" (workspace) with an aria-label for icon-only ToolbarButtons, and keep one size across the row so the controls line up.
- Do: Split a long row into ToolbarGroups with a ToolbarSeparator between them — undo/redo, text style, insert. Groups give the eye the same structure the arrow keys already cross.
- Do: Compose triggers and toggles through ToolbarButton's render prop — render={<MenuTrigger />}, render={<PopoverTrigger />}, or render={<Toggle value="bold" />} inside a ToggleGroup — so they join the toolbar's arrow-key order.
- Don't: Put a bare Button, Toggle or Input inside a Toolbar. It renders, but it is not a toolbar item: the arrow keys skip it and it takes its own tab stop, which is the inconsistency Toolbar exists to remove. Use ToolbarButton, ToolbarInput, or render through ToolbarButton.
- Don't: Wrap one or two buttons, or a dialog's Cancel/Confirm pair, in a Toolbar. Those are independent actions; arrow-key movement there is a surprise, not a shortcut. A plain row of Buttons is right.
- Don't: Use Toolbar for navigation between pages or views. Links that go somewhere are Tabs, SideNav or Breadcrumbs; ToolbarLink is for the odd link that sits among actions, like Help.
- Don't: Give toolbar buttons primary or destructive fills by default. A toolbar is a quiet strip of tools; the ghost default keeps it from competing with the page's one primary action.

### Anatomy

| Part | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Toolbar | yes | The root (role="toolbar"). Owns orientation, loopFocus and disabled for everything inside it. |
| ToolbarButton | yes | An action. Button's ghost variants by default; `render` composes a menu trigger, popover trigger or Toggle into the toolbar. |
| ToolbarGroup | no | A run of related items. `disabled` disables the whole run. |
| ToolbarSeparator | no | A hairline between groups, oriented across the toolbar. Never a focus stop. |
| ToolbarInput | no | A compact Input that joins the arrow-key order — a search or find field in the bar. |
| ToolbarLink | no | An <a> styled like a ToolbarButton, for a link that sits among the actions. |

## Subcomponents

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ToolbarButton | { variant?: buttonVariants variant (default "ghost"); size?: buttonVariants size (default "sm"); disabled?: boolean; focusableWhenDisabled?: boolean (default true); render?: ReactElement } + Base UI Toolbar.Button props | A toolbar action, styled exactly like <Button>. Disabled buttons stay focusable by default and carry aria-disabled. Pass size="icon-sm"/"icon-xs" plus aria-label for icon-only. |
| ToolbarLink | { href?: string; variant?: buttonVariants variant (default "ghost"); size?: buttonVariants size (default "sm"); render?: ReactElement } + Base UI Toolbar.Link props | An <a> in the toolbar's arrow-key order, styled like a ToolbarButton. |
| ToolbarInput | { disabled?: boolean; focusableWhenDisabled?: boolean (default true) } + Base UI Toolbar.Input / native input props | Sable's Input at the sm control height (w-40 by default; override with className). Arrow keys leave the field so it does not trap the row. |
| ToolbarGroup | { disabled?: boolean } + Base UI Toolbar.Group props | Groups related items; `disabled` disables all of them. |
| ToolbarSeparator | Base UI Toolbar.Separator props + className | A hairline-strong rule across the toolbar's axis, exposed as role="separator" and skipped by the arrow keys. |

## Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| orientation | "horizontal" \| "vertical" | "horizontal" | Which arrow keys move focus (Left/Right or Up/Down) and which way the items stack. Separators turn to match. |
| loopFocus | boolean | true | Arrowing past the last item wraps to the first, and back. |
| disabled | boolean | false | Disables every item. Items stay focusable (aria-disabled) so the row keeps its shape under the keyboard. |
| aria-label | string | — | Names the toolbar for assistive technology. Always set it. |
| className | string | — | Layout overrides — e.g. `flex-1` to let the toolbar fill a bar. |

## Variants

- **orientation**: horizontal, vertical
- **variant**: ghost, secondary, outline, primary, destructive, link
- **size**: xs, sm, md, icon, icon-sm, icon-xs

## Tokens used

`foreground`, `accent`, `accent-foreground`, `ring`, `hairline-strong`, `input`, `card`

## Motion

- **arrival** · Toolbar · _no motion_ — A toolbar is fixed chrome. It is present when its surface is; animating it in would leave the tools briefly unusable for no reason the user can see.
- **response** · ToolbarButton · `motion-interactive` — Inherited from buttonVariants: hover fill, focus ring and disabled dim ease together, so the item under the arrow keys reads as the one that moved.
- **response** · ToolbarButton · `motion-press` — Inherited from buttonVariants. Many toolbar actions change something off to the side (the canvas, the selection), so the settle on press is the confirmation that lands where the pointer is.
- **transition** · Toolbar · _no motion_ — The toolbar has no state of its own. Pressed state belongs to a Toggle rendered through ToolbarButton, which carries its own transition.
- **activity** · Toolbar · _no motion_ — A toolbar never works on its own. Pending work belongs to the surface the action targets, or to a Spinner in the button that started it.

## Accessibility

- Base UI renders role="toolbar" with aria-orientation, and a roving tabindex: the toolbar is one tab stop, the arrow keys move between items, Home/End jump to the ends.
- Disabled items stay focusable by default and announce as disabled (aria-disabled), so arrowing along the row never silently skips a control. Set focusableWhenDisabled={false} on an item to opt out.
- ToolbarSeparator is role="separator" with the orientation opposite the toolbar's, and is not a focus stop.
- ToolbarInput lets the arrow keys move the caret and only leaves the field at either end of its text.
- Always set aria-label on the Toolbar, and on every icon-only ToolbarButton.
- A Toggle rendered through ToolbarButton keeps aria-pressed; a MenuTrigger keeps aria-haspopup/aria-expanded.

## Related

- Components: Button, Toggle, Menu, Popover, Tooltip, Workspace, PanelSection, Separator

## Examples

### Formatting toolbar

```tsx
import { Icon, Toggle, ToggleGroup, Toolbar, ToolbarButton, ToolbarGroup, ToolbarLink, ToolbarSeparator } from "@sableui/react"

<Toolbar aria-label="Text formatting">
  <ToolbarGroup aria-label="History">
    <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Undo">
      <Icon name="arrow-left" />
    </ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Redo">
      <Icon name="arrow-right" />
    </ToolbarButton>
  </ToolbarGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToggleGroup multiple aria-label="Style">
    <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Bold" render={<Toggle value="bold" />}>
      <Icon name="bold" />
    </ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Italic" render={<Toggle value="italic" />}>
      <Icon name="italic" />
    </ToolbarButton>
  </ToggleGroup>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarLink href="/help">Help</ToolbarLink>
</Toolbar>
```

### With a menu trigger and a search field

```tsx
import { Menu, MenuContent, MenuItem, MenuTrigger, Toolbar, ToolbarButton, ToolbarInput, ToolbarSeparator } from "@sableui/react"

<Toolbar aria-label="Table">
  <ToolbarButton>Export</ToolbarButton>
  <Menu>
    <ToolbarButton render={<MenuTrigger />}>View</ToolbarButton>
    <MenuContent>
      <MenuItem>Compact rows</MenuItem>
      <MenuItem>Comfortable rows</MenuItem>
    </MenuContent>
  </Menu>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarInput aria-label="Search rows" placeholder="Search" />
</Toolbar>
```

### Vertical tool rail

```tsx
import { Icon, Toolbar, ToolbarButton, ToolbarSeparator } from "@sableui/react"

<Toolbar orientation="vertical" aria-label="Tools">
  <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Select">
    <Icon name="arrow-up" />
  </ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Draw">
    <Icon name="edit" />
  </ToolbarButton>
  <ToolbarSeparator />
  <ToolbarButton size="icon-sm" aria-label="Delete" disabled>
    <Icon name="trash" />
  </ToolbarButton>
</Toolbar>
```

### In a workspace bar

```tsx
import { Icon, Toolbar, ToolbarButton, WorkspaceBar } from "@sableui/react"

<WorkspaceBar>
  <Toolbar aria-label="Document" className="flex-1">
    <ToolbarButton size="xs">File</ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton size="xs">Edit</ToolbarButton>
    <ToolbarButton size="icon-xs" aria-label="Share" className="ms-auto">
      <Icon name="share" />
    </ToolbarButton>
  </Toolbar>
</WorkspaceBar>
```

# Tooltip

**Status:** stable

Hover/focus label over Base UI Tooltip (collision-aware positioning, ARIA wiring, delay grouping via TooltipProvider). Compact popover surface.

**Keywords:** tooltip, hint, hover, assistive

## Usage

Use Tooltip for brief nonessential hints tied to a specific control or piece of text.

### Best practices

- Do: Use it to name icon-only controls or clarify compact UI when the label cannot be visible.
- Do: Keep tooltip content short and noninteractive.
- Don't: Do not put critical instructions, errors, or interactive content inside Tooltip.
- Don't: Do not let a tooltip serve as an icon button's accessible name. A tooltip is not a name — without its own aria-label the button announces as "button", and the tooltip never opens for a screen reader at all.

### Anatomy

| Part | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TooltipProvider | no | Optional provider for shared tooltip timing. |
| TooltipTrigger | yes | The element that owns the hint. |
| TooltipContent | yes | The short hint content. |
| TooltipArrow | no | An optional pointer toward the trigger. |
| SimpleTooltip | no | A convenience wrapper for common tooltip usage. |

## Subcomponents

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TooltipProvider | Base UI Tooltip.Provider props (delay, closeDelay, timeout) | Wraps an app or group of Tooltips to share open/close delays. Once one tooltip is open, adjacent tooltips open instantly. |
| TooltipTrigger | Base UI Trigger props + render | The anchor element. Use render={<Button/>} to compose with another component. |
| TooltipContent | Base UI Popup props + side \| align \| sideOffset + className | Portals + positions + paints the popup. side ("top" \| "bottom" \| "left" \| "right" \| "inline-*") picks which side of the trigger to render against, defaults to "top", and auto-flips on collision; align ("start" \| "center" \| "end") defaults to "center"; sideOffset (gap between trigger and popup, in pixels) defaults to 6. |
| TooltipArrow | Base UI Arrow props + className | Optional pointer connecting the popup to its trigger — a popover-coloured square turned 45° that carries the border on its outward edges. Place inside TooltipContent. |
| SimpleTooltip | Base UI Tooltip.Root props + content: ReactNode + children: ReactElement + side \| align \| sideOffset | Shorthand wrapping Root + Trigger + Content for the common case. The single child becomes the trigger (via Base UI render); content sets the body; side / align / sideOffset forward to the content with the same defaults. Composition parts remain for advanced use. |

## Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| side | "top" \| "right" \| "bottom" \| "left" | "top" | On TooltipContent: which side of the trigger to render against. Flips automatically when there is no room. |
| Tooltip (Root) | Base UI Tooltip.Root props (open, defaultOpen, onOpenChange, disabled) | — | Groups the trigger and content. Uncontrolled by default. |

## Tokens used

`popover`, `popover-foreground`, `border-floating`

## Motion

- **arrival** · Content · `motion-pop` — The transform-origin follows the anchor, so the tooltip appears to grow out of the element it describes. That is what binds it to its trigger — a bubble that materialises at full size near two possible triggers belongs to neither.
- **response** · Content · _no motion_ — The tooltip is not a hover target; pointing at it is how you dismiss it. Styling it for the pointer would suggest otherwise.
- **transition** · Content · `motion-pop` — Same recipe, exit direction — it collapses back toward the anchor. Content that fades from a fixed size on close reads as a second, unrelated element disappearing.
- **activity** · Content · _no motion_ — Tooltip copy is resident before the tooltip opens. Anything that has to be fetched is a Popover with its own loading state.

## Accessibility

- Base UI wires aria-describedby from trigger to popup and manages hover + focus open.
- Opens on keyboard focus, not just hover; dismisses on Esc and blur.
- Animate via data-[starting-style]/data-[ending-style] opacity attributes.
- Tooltip text is supplementary — never put essential-only actions inside a tooltip.

## Related

- Components: Popover, ContextCard

## Examples

### Basic

```tsx
import { Button, Icon, Tooltip, TooltipContent, TooltipProvider, TooltipTrigger } from "@sableui/react"

<TooltipProvider><Tooltip><TooltipTrigger render={<Button variant="ghost" size="icon-sm" aria-label="Info"><Icon name="info" /></Button>} /><TooltipContent>Stored permanently on Arweave.</TooltipContent></Tooltip></TooltipProvider>
```

### Sides

```tsx
import { Button, Tooltip, TooltipContent, TooltipTrigger } from "@sableui/react"

<Tooltip><TooltipTrigger render={<Button variant="secondary">Right</Button>} /><TooltipContent side="right">Opens to the right</TooltipContent></Tooltip>
```

### Shorthand (SimpleTooltip)

```tsx
import { Button, Icon, SimpleTooltip } from "@sableui/react"

<SimpleTooltip content="Stored permanently on Arweave."><Button variant="ghost" size="icon-sm" aria-label="Info"><Icon name="info" /></Button></SimpleTooltip>
```

# Tree

**Status:** stable

The object list a tool is built around — layers, scene graph, outline — on one shared grid, so every left edge in the panel resolves to the rail or an exact multiple of the indent step.

**Keywords:** tree, layers, outline, scene graph, hierarchy, nesting, indent, disclosure, workspace, panel, file tree, files, folders, explorer, treeview

## Usage

Use Tree for the hierarchy panel in a workspace: layers, objects, an inspector outline. It owns the geometry that makes nesting legible — the rail, the disclosure and type columns, and the indent step — via the density ladder (scope the panel with data-density, e.g. data-density="compact"), so nothing in the panel computes its own inset. It is also the file tree: nest rows with `subtree`, let folders manage their own open state with `defaultExpanded`, and mark kind with the `icon` convention (folder for a row with a subtree, file for a leaf). Reach for Accordion when the content is prose sections rather than nodes in a hierarchy.

### Best practices

- Do: Give Tree an aria-label naming the hierarchy ("Layers", "Files"). It is a role="tree", and an unnamed tree is announced as just "tree".
- Do: For a file tree, nest with `subtree` and use the icon convention: `icon={<Icon name="folder" />}` on a row with a subtree, `icon={<Icon name="file" />}` on a leaf. There are no folder/file presets — they would only bind those two props.
- Do: Give TreeAddRow the same depth as the rows it adds to, so its mark lands in their type column: one deeper than the parent for a child list, the parent's own depth for a sibling list.
- Do: Put mutable per-row state (visibility, solo, a row menu) in `actions`, on the right rail. Show it on hover with `reveal-on-hover` (the row is its `group`), and at rest only when its value is the non-default one.
- Do: Let section headers sit on the rail at the same height as a depth-0 row. Space and a hairline separate sections; TreeSection handles both, including dropping the divider on the first.
- Don't: Hardcode a left inset anywhere in the panel. Use treeIndent(depth) or var(--tree-rail); a hand-written px value is how a tree ends up with four different left edges.
- Don't: Redefine --tree-indent to anything other than --tree-column. A step smaller than the column puts a child's content left of its parent's and the nesting reads inverted.
- Don't: Put the visibility toggle before the name. A leading toggle makes each row's visual start depend on its depth, so no two rows share an edge.
- Don't: Hand-copy icon paths into a tree row. Use Icon and the shared semantic set, or provide an app-specific icon through the supported slot.
- Don't: Use EmptyState inside a panel. It is page-register furniture (px-6 py-12 around a size-12 disc) and in 240px it spends 24px of inset and ~96px of height on nothing. Use TreeEmpty.
- Don't: Show explanatory prose AND an add row in an empty section. That is two things to read where one carries the affordance; give TreeEmpty a one-line message and pass the add row as its action.
- Don't: Leave a section actionable when its action cannot do anything yet — a document-level effect list with no content to apply to, for instance. Hide the section or its affordance until the thing it operates on exists.

### Anatomy

| Part | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tree | yes | The container. Does not scroll itself — put it in a scrolling Panel, or make it the scrolling region with className. |
| TreeSection | no | A titled group. Header on the rail, hairline above, divider suppressed on the first section. |
| TreeRow | yes | One node: rail, disclosure column, type column, name, right-rail actions. |
| TreeAddRow | no | The affordance that ends a branch. Mark in the type column, label in the name column. |
| TreeEmpty | no | A section's empty state at panel scale: one line, one action, optionally a dashed drop region. |

## Subcomponents

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TreeSection | { title: ReactNode; hint?: string; action?: ReactNode } | A titled group of rows, with the header on the rail. |
| TreeRow | { depth?: number; selected?: boolean; accent?: boolean; dimmed?: boolean; expandable?: boolean; expanded?: boolean; defaultExpanded?: boolean; onExpandedChange?: (expanded: boolean) => void; subtree?: ReactNode; toggleLabel?: string; disclosureIcon?: ReactNode; icon?: ReactNode; actions?: ReactNode } | One node in the hierarchy (role=treeitem inside a Tree). Controlled via expanded/onExpandedChange or uncontrolled via defaultExpanded; nest children with subtree. Always reserves both leading columns (disclosure and type), so a leaf's name lines up with its expandable siblings. |
| TreeAddRow | { depth?: number; label: ReactNode; icon?: ReactNode } | The add affordance, shaped as a row and aligned to the branch it adds to. Its mark sits in the type column (level with the siblings' kind markers), not the name column. `icon` replaces the built-in add mark. |
| TreeEmpty | { message: ReactNode; action?: ReactNode; dropTarget?: boolean; depth?: number } | A section's or a branch's empty state, at panel scale rather than page scale. One-line message, one action slot; dropTarget renders it as a dashed drop region and sets data-drop-target for styling. `depth` (inherited inside a subtree) starts the line on the edge of the rows that branch would hold. |
| treeIndent | (depth: number) => string | The left inset for a depth, as a calc() expression reading the density ladder. Use this rather than computing pixels. |

## Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| depth | number | 0 | Nesting level, on TreeRow and TreeAddRow. 0 sits on the rail; each level adds one --tree-indent. |
| expandable | boolean | true with subtree, else false | Whether TreeRow renders a disclosure control. The column is reserved either way, so leaf and parent names stay aligned. |
| expanded | boolean | — | Controlled open state for a TreeRow. Pair with onExpandedChange; omit both for an uncontrolled row. |
| defaultExpanded | boolean | true | Uncontrolled initial open state, used when `expanded` is not passed. Pass false for a file tree's closed folders. |
| onExpandedChange | (expanded: boolean) => void | — | Called when a TreeRow opens or closes — from the disclosure, ArrowRight/ArrowLeft, or activating a row that has no onClick. Fires in both controlled and uncontrolled use. |
| subtree | ReactNode | — | The rows nested under a TreeRow, rendered after it while it is expanded. Nested rows inherit depth + 1 unless they pass their own `depth`, so a file tree never computes depth by hand. |
| selected | boolean | false | Selection fill and accent bar on a TreeRow. Inside a Tree it is exposed as aria-selected on the treeitem; a row rendered outside a Tree is a plain div and exposes aria-current instead. |
| toggleLabel | string | — | Names the thing being disclosed, for the toggle's accessible label — "Expand Background" rather than "Expand group". Every example passes it; a screen-reader user hearing twenty identical "Expand group" buttons has no way to tell them apart. |
| icon | ReactNode | — | The kind marker for a TreeRow, rendered in the type column at 1em. Use a semantic Icon so it follows the app icon set. |
| disclosureIcon | ReactNode | — | Replaces TreeRow's semantic chevron-down icon. Omit to use the chevron-down from the app's IconProvider set. |
| actions | ReactNode | — | Right-rail controls for a TreeRow: visibility, solo, a row menu. |
| label | ReactNode | — | TreeAddRow's visible label. Name what gets added — 'Add effect', not 'Add'. |

## Tokens used

`panel-raised`, `hairline`, `foreground`, `muted-foreground`, `primary`, `ring`

## Accessibility

- Tree implements the ARIA tree view pattern: Tree is role="tree", each TreeRow and TreeAddRow is role="treeitem" with aria-level, expandable rows carry aria-expanded, and a TreeSection is a role="group" labelled by its heading. Rows stay flat in the DOM — hierarchy is aria-level — so the fills span the panel's full width.
- Keyboard: exactly one row is in the tab order (roving tabindex, seeded on the selected row, else the first). ArrowUp/Down move between visible rows; ArrowRight expands a collapsed row, then steps to its first child; ArrowLeft collapses an expanded row, else steps to its parent; Home/End jump to the ends; Enter/Space activate the row — its onClick, or toggling it when it has none. Keys pressed inside a row's own controls (an action button, a rename field) are left to that control.
- Selection has one mapping: inside a Tree, `selected` is aria-selected on the treeitem; outside a Tree the row is a plain div, where aria-selected is invalid, so it falls back to aria-current. A navigation tree that wants aria-current="page" passes it through props.
- Each treeitem is named by its own label (aria-labelledby the name), never by the text of its icon or action buttons.
- The disclosure is a real button with aria-expanded and a label naming what it discloses, and it stops propagation so collapsing a group never changes the selection. Inside a Tree the treeitem carries aria-expanded and the arrow keys, so the button becomes a pointer target only: aria-hidden, out of the tab order, and it leaves focus where it was when clicked.
- The disclosure's POINTER TARGET is bigger than the mark it draws. `--tree-column` is 20px comfortable and 18px compact, both under WCAG 2.5.8's 24x24 floor, so a centred pseudo-element takes the hit at `--control-xs` (28/24) instead. The drawn box stays on the column, because that column is also the indent step — growing the button would push every name in the tree one column right.
- Right-rail actions stay in the tab order, so a row with actions costs extra Tab stops. Keep actions few and reveal them with `reveal-on-hover`, which also shows them on focus and always on touch.
- `dimmed` is presentation only. A row switched off must also say so in its actions' aria-pressed or its accessible name; opacity alone is invisible to a screen reader and fails contrast.
- Right-rail controls that appear on hover must also appear on focus-visible, or they are unreachable by keyboard.

## Related

- Components: Panel, PanelSection, Workspace, Accordion, SideNav

## Examples

### File tree

```tsx
import { Icon, Tree, TreeRow } from "@sableui/react"

// Nest with subtree; folders own their open state via defaultExpanded.
// A row with no onClick toggles when clicked or activated, like a folder in
// a file explorer. Depth is inherited — never computed by hand.
<Tree aria-label="Files" className="max-w-xs">
  <TreeRow
    icon={<Icon name="folder" />}
    toggleLabel="src"
    subtree={
      <>
        <TreeRow icon={<Icon name="file" />} onClick={() => open("index.ts")}>index.ts</TreeRow>
        <TreeRow
          icon={<Icon name="folder" />}
          toggleLabel="components"
          defaultExpanded={false}
          subtree={
            <TreeRow icon={<Icon name="file" />} selected onClick={() => open("button.tsx")}>
              button.tsx
            </TreeRow>
          }
        >
          components
        </TreeRow>
      </>
    }
  >
    src
  </TreeRow>
  <TreeRow icon={<Icon name="file" />} onClick={() => open("README.md")}>README.md</TreeRow>
</Tree>
```

### Layer tree with per-node effects

```tsx
import { Button, Icon, Tree, TreeAddRow, TreeRow, TreeSection } from "@sableui/react"

<Tree aria-label="Layers" className="min-h-0 flex-1 overflow-y-auto scrollbar-quiet">
  <TreeSection title="Document effects" hint="Applied to the flattened composite">
    <TreeRow depth={0} icon={<Icon name="sparkles" />}>Channel shift</TreeRow>
    <TreeAddRow depth={0} label="Add effect" />
  </TreeSection>

  <TreeSection title="Layers" action={<span className="text-ui-num text-muted-foreground">2</span>}>
    <TreeRow
      depth={0}
      expandable
      expanded
      toggleLabel="Backdrop"
      icon={<Icon name="image-stack" />}
      actions={<Button size="icon-xs" variant="ghost" aria-label="Hide Backdrop"><Icon name="eye" /></Button>}
    >
      Backdrop
    </TreeRow>
    <TreeRow depth={1} icon={<Icon name="sparkles" />}>Block displacement</TreeRow>
    <TreeAddRow depth={1} label="Add effect" />

    <TreeRow depth={0} icon={<Icon name="image-stack" />} dimmed>Overlay</TreeRow>
    <TreeAddRow depth={0} label="Add image" />
  </TreeSection>
</Tree>
```

### Empty state — one line, one action

```tsx
import { TreeAddRow, TreeEmpty, TreeSection } from "@sableui/react"

// A section with nothing in it offers exactly ONE way forward. Not EmptyState:
// that is page-register (px-6 py-12 around a size-12 disc) and in a 240px panel
// it spends 24px of inset and ~96px of height on nothing.
<TreeSection title="Layers">
  <TreeEmpty message="No images yet" action={<TreeAddRow depth={0} label="Add image" />} />
</TreeSection>

// As a drop region — the app owns the drag handlers; TreeEmpty owns the frame
// and sets data-drop-target so a data-[drop-active] style can respond.
<TreeEmpty
  dropTarget
  message="Drop an image"
  data-drop-active={dragging || undefined}
  onDragOver={(e) => { e.preventDefault(); setDragging(true) }}
  onDragLeave={() => setDragging(false)}
  onDrop={handleDrop}
  className="data-[drop-active]:border-primary"
/>
```

### Selection and disclosure

```tsx
import { Icon, Tree, TreeRow } from "@sableui/react"

<Tree aria-label="Layers">
  <TreeRow
    depth={0}
    expandable
    expanded={open}
    onExpandedChange={setOpen}
    toggleLabel="Group 1"
    icon={<Icon name="folder" />}
    selected
    onClick={() => select("group-1")}
  >
    Group 1
  </TreeRow>
  {open ? <TreeRow depth={1} icon={<Icon name="file" />}>Child</TreeRow> : null}
</Tree>
```

### An empty branch

```tsx
import { Icon, TreeAddRow, TreeEmpty, TreeRow } from "@sableui/react"

// A layer with no effects: TreeEmpty at the branch's depth lands on the
// same edge its effect rows would — no hand-computed inset.
<TreeRow depth={0} icon={<Icon name="image-stack" />} toggleLabel="Overlay" subtree={
  <>
    <TreeEmpty message="No effects yet" />
    <TreeAddRow label="Add effect" />
  </>
}>
  Overlay
</TreeRow>
```

### Aligning a custom affordance

```tsx
import { treeIndent } from "@sableui/react"

// Anything else that needs a tree inset reads it from the same place the rows do.
<div style={{ paddingInlineStart: treeIndent(1) }} className="flex h-(--control-xs) items-center">
  <span className="text-ui-body text-muted-foreground">Drag a layer here</span>
</div>
```

# Video

**Status:** stable

Styled 16:9 video player frame. Mounts a native <video> when given a src, or shows a poster/placeholder with a centered play overlay.

**Keywords:** video, media, player, demo

## Usage

Use Video to embed playable or previewable video media inside a page.

### Best practices

- Do: Use captions, poster imagery, and controls when the video carries information.
- Do: Keep the surrounding layout stable while media loads.
- Don't: Do not autoplay important audio or make video the only way to access required information.
- Don't: Do not ship it without captions or a transcript. Captions are what make video usable for deaf users and searchable for everyone; a video with neither is inaccessible content you also cannot index.

## Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| onRequestPlay | () => void | — | Placeholder only (no src): renders the play mark as a real button labelled "Play video" that calls this — e.g. to load the source. Without it the mark is decorative. |
| src | string | — | Video source URL. When omitted, a poster/placeholder with a play overlay renders. |
| poster | string | — | Poster image shown before playback (and as the placeholder backdrop). |
| controls | boolean | true | Show native playback controls. |

## Tokens used

`border`, `overlay`, `overlay-foreground`, `ring`

## Accessibility

- Mounts a native <video> element, preserving built-in keyboard controls when controls is enabled.
- Without onRequestPlay the placeholder play mark is decorative (aria-hidden) — nothing on the frame pretends to be pressable. With it, the mark is a native button named "Play video".

## Related

- Components: Carousel, Dialog, Badge

## Examples

### With a poster

```tsx
import { Video } from "@sableui/react"

<Video poster="/cover.jpg" src="/clip.mp4" />
```

### Placeholder (no src)

```tsx
import { Video } from "@sableui/react"

<Video poster="/cover.jpg" />
```

### Placeholder that loads on play

```tsx
import { Video } from "@sableui/react"

<Video poster="/cover.jpg" src={src} onRequestPlay={() => setSrc("/clip.mp4")} />
```

# Workspace

**Status:** stable

The shell for a tool: a fixed viewport partitioned into independently scrolling regions, with a compact density scope, a skip link, and a canvas landmark.

**Keywords:** workspace, tool, editor, shell, frame, canvas, chrome, panels, density, viewport

## Usage

Use Workspace as the outer frame for a tool — an editor, a console, a canvas app. It owns the viewport, scopes the compact control density, and guarantees a skip link plus a main landmark on the canvas. Reach for AppShell instead for page-register products: it is built around a scrolling document, where a workspace is built around a fixed one. Workspace fills the viewport (h-dvh) by design; to embed one in a page (a docs preview, a modal-sized demo), wrap it in a bounded container and pass className="h-full".

### Best practices

- Do: Put a PanelGroup in the body and a WorkspaceCanvas inside it, so panels are aside chrome and the work surface is the main landmark.
- Do: Let each panel own its scrolling. The shell never scrolls, and the canvas clips rather than scrolls — panning is the viewport's job.
- Do: Keep the density scope at compact unless you have a specific reason; the workspace register's measured control ladder is what makes tool chrome read as tool chrome.
- Don't: Nest a Region or Page inside it to set a width. Region caps are a page-register idea; a workspace is edge-to-edge and its panels are fixed-width chrome outside the content grid.
- Don't: Hardcode a control height (h-[32px]). CI rejects it (raw-control-height); read the ladder instead, e.g. h-(--control-sm), so the density scope can size it.
- Don't: Put a Card in the chrome. Use PanelSection — a card inside a narrow panel spends its border and inset on nothing.
- Don't: Use it for a dashboard that scrolls. If the primary interaction is reading down a page, that's AppShell plus a Region, not a workspace.

### Anatomy

| Part | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WorkspaceBar | no | Top chrome at --chrome-bar-height with a hairline beneath: toolbar, document tabs, menubar row. |
| Body | yes | The flexible middle row, normally a PanelGroup. Constrained so its children can shrink and scroll. |
| WorkspaceCanvas | no | The work surface and the main#main-content landmark the skip link targets. Clips rather than scrolls. |
| StatusBar | no | Bottom chrome for ambient document facts. |

## Subcomponents

| Name | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WorkspaceBar | ComponentProps<'header'> | The top chrome strip, sized to --chrome-bar-height with a hairline beneath. |
| WorkspaceCanvas | ComponentProps<'main'> | The work surface: renders main#main-content, fills the body, clips its overflow. |

## Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| toolbar | ReactNode | — | Top chrome, normally a WorkspaceBar. |
| statusBar | ReactNode | — | Bottom chrome, normally a StatusBar. |
| density | "compact" \| "comfortable" | "compact" | Density scope for everything inside. Sets the --control-* ladder via data-density; compact is the workspace register. Nothing hardcodes a height, so the same size="md" Button is 40px on a page and 32px inside a compact Workspace. A Dialog opened from inside resets to comfortable, because a modal is a page-register surface even when a tool launched it. |
| skipLinkLabel | string | "Skip to canvas" | Text for the skip link that targets the canvas landmark. |

## Tokens used

`canvas`, `canvas-foreground`, `panel`, `hairline`, `popover`, `popover-foreground`, `ring`

## Accessibility

- Renders a skip link to #main-content as the first focusable element, even though there is no scrolling document.
- WorkspaceCanvas is the <main id="main-content"> landmark; Panels are <aside> chrome with their own names.
- Density only changes control sizes, never hit-target rules — an icon button at the 24px floor still needs a padded 44px hit area.

## Related

- Components: PanelGroup, PanelSection, StatusBar, ScrubField, AppShell

## Examples

### Editor shell

```tsx
import { Button, Panel, PanelGroup, PanelSection, PropertyPair, PropertyRow, ScrubField, Separator, StatusBar, StatusBarGroup, StatusBarSeparator, Switch, Workspace, WorkspaceBar, WorkspaceCanvas } from "@sableui/react"

<Workspace
  toolbar={
    <WorkspaceBar>
      <span className="px-1 text-ui-md text-foreground">Studio</span>
      <Separator orientation="vertical" className="mx-1 h-4" />
      <Button size="xs" variant="ghost">Open</Button>
    </WorkspaceBar>
  }
  statusBar={
    <StatusBar>
      <span className="text-ui-num">1024 × 768</span>
      <StatusBarSeparator />
      <span>3 layers</span>
      <StatusBarGroup align="end"><span>Saved</span></StatusBarGroup>
    </StatusBar>
  }
>
  <PanelGroup>
    <Panel label="Layers" width={240}>
      <PanelSection title="Layers">
        <PropertyRow label="Background"><Switch defaultChecked /></PropertyRow>
      </PanelSection>
    </Panel>
    <WorkspaceCanvas>
      <div className="grid h-full place-items-center text-ui-body text-muted-foreground">Canvas</div>
    </WorkspaceCanvas>
    <Panel label="Properties" width={256}>
      <PanelSection title="Blending">
        <PropertyPair>
          <ScrubField label="Opacity" icon="grid" suffix="%" value={100} min={0} max={100} />
          <ScrubField label="Blur" value={0} min={0} max={64} suffix="px" />
        </PropertyPair>
      </PanelSection>
    </Panel>
  </PanelGroup>
</Workspace>
```

### Console shell (no canvas)

```tsx

```

### Comfortable density

```tsx

<Workspace density="comfortable" toolbar={<WorkspaceBar><span className="text-ui-md">Review</span></WorkspaceBar>}>
  <PanelGroup>
    <WorkspaceCanvas>
      <div className="grid h-full place-items-center text-body-md text-muted-foreground">Touch-friendly review mode</div>
    </WorkspaceCanvas>
  </PanelGroup>
</Workspace>
```

## Token intent

Which token to reach for, and what it is most often confused with. Generated from `src/themes/token-docs.ts`; the full data is `registry.json → tokens`.

### semantic (49)

- **`background`** — The page. The furthest-back surface in the page register. *Use for:* The document body, and any surface meant to read as 'the page itself'. Never anything that floats: background is the BOTTOM of the surface stack (background < card < popover in every dark mode), so a floating panel painted with it reads as a hole beneath the cards it hovers over.
    - **Not** `popover` for anything floating, `card` for a bounded block on the page. `canvas`. `canvas` is the *work* surface in a tool — the artboard being edited — which is not the page behind the UI. Using `background` for an artboard makes the thing being edited indistinguishable from the chrome around it.
- **`foreground`** — The default ink, for `background`. *Use for:* Body text and any content sitting directly on the page.
    - **Not** any other surface's ink. On `card`, `popover`, `panel` or a tone, use that surface's own `-foreground`.
- **`card`** — A raised content container on the page. *Use for:* A bounded block of related content on a page: an article teaser, a settings group, a stat panel.
    - **Not** `popover`. A card sits *in* the document flow; a popover floats above it and needs its own elevation and border treatment. And never inside a docked panel — use `panel` surfaces and `PanelSection`; a card in a 240px panel spends its border and inset on nothing. Never rely on `card` as a FILL to separate something from the page: a preset's `card` can equal `background`, because a card separates by its border. A track, well or pad that must read with no border is `muted`.
- **`card-foreground`** — Ink paired with `card`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `card`. Use them as a pair — `bg-card text-card-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`popover`** — A floating surface: menu, popover, tooltip body, select list, dialog, and any persistent floating panel (an inspector, a toolbar over a canvas). *Use for:* Anything rendered in a layer above the page that needs its own background, dismissible or not. The test is elevation: if it floats over content (`shadow-md` or higher, fixed or absolutely positioned above the page), it is popover. Pair with `text-popover-foreground`.
    - **Not** `card` and `background`. The distinction is elevation, not shape or lifetime: a panel that stays open is still floating. `background` is the page ground and `card` sits on it; both read as sunk under a floating panel. In light mode several presets make all three equal, so a floating surface also needs its edge (ring or border) and shadow, never the fill alone.
- **`popover-foreground`** — Ink paired with `popover`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `popover`. Use them as a pair — `bg-popover text-popover-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`muted`** — A recessed surface. Quieter than the page, not interactive. *Use for:* An inset well: a code block background, a disabled field, a read-only region, a table's zebra stripe, a segmented-control track. On the page it always differs from `background`. Inside any OTHER surface (a card, a popover, a floating panel) use the `sable-well` utility instead: it derives the well from the surface it sits in, so it is the same visible step everywhere, whereas `muted` can land within a step of a popover in some dark modes. Never compensate with an outline on every well — that turns a panel into a stack of boxes.
    - **Not** `secondary` and `accent`. All three are near-identical in most themes, which is exactly why the rule is by ROLE: `muted` is *recessed and inert*, `secondary` is a *control fill*, `accent` is a *transient state*. Pick by what the surface does, never by which looks right — they diverge in other themes.
- **`muted-foreground`** — De-emphasised ink. The single most-used token after `foreground`. *Use for:* Secondary text: captions, helper text, placeholder-adjacent labels, a property name next to its value, timestamps.
    - **Not** `foreground` at reduced opacity. Opacity on text compounds unpredictably against whatever is behind it and can fall below the contrast floor; this token is a tuned value that does not.
- **`border`** — The default hairline. Tuned to be subtle. *Use for:* Input outlines, badge edges, card borders — chrome that should not draw the eye.
    - **Not** `border-strong`. Reach for `border-strong` when the line carries *structure* (a grid rule, a table divider, a section separator) and for `border` when it merely bounds a control.
- **`border-strong`** — A structural divider. Visibly stronger than `border`. *Use for:* Grid lines, table rules, separators between major sections.
    - **Not** `border`. If removing the line would make the layout ambiguous, it is structural and belongs here.
- **`input`** — The outline of a form control specifically. *Use for:* Text inputs, textareas and selects. Not the edge of a checkbox, radio or switch — that is `control-border`.
    - **Not** `border`. They are often the same value, but a theme is entitled to make form controls read differently from other chrome, and only this token gives it the hook.
- **`control-border`** — The resting edge of a control whose outline is the whole control. Held to 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.11) on every surface. *Use for:* An unchecked checkbox, an unselected radio, an off switch track, a selection card's check or radio mark — anywhere removing the edge would make the control disappear.
    - **Not** `input`. A text field is also found by its fill, caret and placeholder, so its outline may stay quiet; a checkbox has nothing else, and at `input`'s strength it measures about 1.4:1.
- **`ring`** — The focus indicator colour. *Use for:* Only for `focus-visible`. Nothing else.
    - **Not** `primary`. Focus must remain distinguishable from selection; if the ring is the same colour as a selected state, a keyboard user cannot tell where focus is.
- **`primary`** — The one high-emphasis action colour. *Use for:* The single most important action on a surface — one per view. A submit button, the primary CTA.
    - **Not** `accent`. `primary` says *do this*; `accent` says *this is the current one*. Two primary buttons on one screen means neither is primary.
- **`primary-foreground`** — Ink paired with `primary`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `primary`. Use them as a pair — `bg-primary text-primary-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`secondary`** — A lower-emphasis control fill. *Use for:* A secondary button, a segmented control's resting fill, a neutral chip.
    - **Not** `muted`. `secondary` is for something you can *press*; `muted` is for a surface that is inert. See the `muted` note — role, not appearance.
- **`secondary-foreground`** — Ink paired with `secondary`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `secondary`. Use them as a pair — `bg-secondary text-secondary-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`accent`** — A transient state fill: hover, selected, current. *Use for:* The fill behind a hovered menu item, a selected list row, the active segment of a switcher.
    - **Not** `primary` for selection, and `muted` for hover. `accent` is the state layer; the other two are emphasis and recession respectively.
- **`accent-foreground`** — Ink paired with `accent`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `accent`. Use them as a pair — `bg-accent text-accent-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`destructive`** — Irreversible or data-losing actions. *Use for:* Delete, revoke, remove, discard — and the error state of a form field.
    - **Not** `tone-warning`. Destructive means *this destroys something*; warning means *be careful*. A confirmation dialog's action is destructive; the banner explaining it is a warning.
- **`destructive-foreground`** — Ink paired with `destructive`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `destructive`. Use them as a pair — `bg-destructive text-destructive-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`success`** — A confirmed, completed, healthy state. *Use for:* A passing check, a saved indicator, a healthy status dot.
    - **Not** `tone-info`. Success asserts an outcome; info asserts a fact. 'Saved' is success, '3 items' is info.
- **`success-foreground`** — Ink paired with `success`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `success`. Use them as a pair — `bg-success text-success-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`tone-standard`** — Domain tone: the baseline classification in a set. Part of the `tone-*` family, which exists so a product can classify content without inventing colours per feature. *Use for:* The default category of a classified item — the one that means 'nothing special'.
    - **Not** `muted`. A tone is *semantic classification* that a reader is meant to decode; `muted` is de-emphasis. If a legend would help the user, it is a tone.
- **`tone-collectible`** — Domain tone: a scarce or owned item. *Use for:* Marking an item as collectible/owned in a classified set.
    - **Not** `primary`. A tone classifies the *thing*; primary drives an *action*. A collectible badge is not a button.
- **`tone-edition`** — Domain tone: an edition or release. *Use for:* Marking editioned content in a classified set.
    - **Not** `tone-collectible`. Distinct classifications must stay visually distinct.
- **`tone-info`** — Domain tone: neutral, factual information. *Use for:* An informational note or banner, a neutral count, a 'did you know' surface.
    - **Not** `success`. Info states a fact; success states an outcome. Also not `primary` — an info banner is not an action.
- **`tone-warning`** — Domain tone: proceed with care, nothing is broken yet. *Use for:* A caution banner, a nearing-limit indicator, a soloed/overridden state in a tool.
    - **Not** `destructive`. Warning is *advisory*; destructive is *consequential*. If nothing is lost by continuing, it is a warning.
- **`highlight`** — A marker on content the user is meant to notice — search hits, diffs, annotations. *Use for:* Highlighting matched text, a changed line, a called-out passage.
    - **Not** `accent`. `accent` is UI state that follows the pointer or selection; `highlight` marks the *content* and persists independently of interaction.
- **`tone-standard-foreground`** — Ink paired with `tone-standard`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `tone-standard`. Use them as a pair — `bg-tone-standard text-tone-standard-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`tone-collectible-foreground`** — Ink paired with `tone-collectible`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `tone-collectible`. Use them as a pair — `bg-tone-collectible text-tone-collectible-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`tone-edition-foreground`** — Ink paired with `tone-edition`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `tone-edition`. Use them as a pair — `bg-tone-edition text-tone-edition-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`tone-info-foreground`** — Ink paired with `tone-info`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `tone-info`. Use them as a pair — `bg-tone-info text-tone-info-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`tone-warning-foreground`** — Ink paired with `tone-warning`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `tone-warning`. Use them as a pair — `bg-tone-warning text-tone-warning-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`highlight-foreground`** — Ink paired with `highlight`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `highlight`. Use them as a pair — `bg-highlight text-highlight-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`destructive-text`** — `destructive` drawn on a surface: text, icons, borders and focus rings. *Use for:* Write `text-destructive`, `border-destructive` or `ring-destructive` — they read this token; only `bg-destructive` reads the fill.
    - **Not** `destructive` itself for marks on a page. The fill is tuned to carry a label (dark mode lowers it under white ink), which can leave it too dark to read on a dark card.
- **`success-text`** — `success` drawn on a surface: text, icons, borders and focus rings. *Use for:* Write `text-success`, `border-success` or `ring-success` — they read this token; only `bg-success` reads the fill.
    - **Not** `success` itself for marks on a page. The fill is tuned to carry a label (dark mode lowers it under white ink), which can leave it too dark to read on a dark card.
- **`tone-warning-text`** — `tone-warning` drawn on a surface: text, icons, borders and focus rings. *Use for:* Write `text-tone-warning`, `border-tone-warning` or `ring-tone-warning` — they read this token; only `bg-tone-warning` reads the fill.
    - **Not** `tone-warning` itself for marks on a page. The fill is tuned to carry a label (dark mode lowers it under white ink), which can leave it too dark to read on a dark card.
- **`tone-info-text`** — `tone-info` drawn on a surface: text, icons, borders and focus rings. *Use for:* Write `text-tone-info`, `border-tone-info` or `ring-tone-info` — they read this token; only `bg-tone-info` reads the fill.
    - **Not** `tone-info` itself for marks on a page. The fill is tuned to carry a label (dark mode lowers it under white ink), which can leave it too dark to read on a dark card.
- **`overlay`** — A scrim over the page behind a modal, and the wash behind media chrome. *Use for:* Dialog and sheet backdrops, letterboxing, a pill sitting on top of an image.
    - **Not** `bg-black/50`. Pure black is never right — it crushes whatever is behind it, and a theme cannot tune it. This token is the sanctioned answer, which is why `raw-black-white` is a lint rule.
- **`overlay-foreground`** — Ink paired with `overlay`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `overlay`. Use them as a pair — `bg-overlay text-overlay-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`sidebar`** — The app sidebar's own surface. Heads a small family (`sidebar-*`) that lets navigation chrome diverge from the page without overriding page tokens. *Use for:* The `Sidebar` / `SideNav` background.
    - **Not** `card`. A sidebar is persistent chrome, not content — a theme frequently wants it a different tone from the cards inside the page it frames.
- **`sidebar-foreground`** — Ink paired with `sidebar`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `sidebar`. Use them as a pair — `bg-sidebar text-sidebar-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`sidebar-primary`** — The high-emphasis colour *within* the sidebar. *Use for:* The active nav item's fill, when the sidebar has its own tonal world.
    - **Not** `primary`. Page primary on a sidebar surface may not clear contrast; this token is tuned against `sidebar`.
- **`sidebar-primary-foreground`** — Ink paired with `sidebar-primary`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `sidebar-primary`. Use them as a pair — `bg-sidebar-primary text-sidebar-primary-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`sidebar-accent`** — The state layer within the sidebar — hover, current. *Use for:* Hovered or current nav items.
    - **Not** `accent`, for the same contrast reason as `sidebar-primary`.
- **`sidebar-accent-foreground`** — Ink paired with `sidebar-accent`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `sidebar-accent`. Use them as a pair — `bg-sidebar-accent text-sidebar-accent-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`sidebar-border`** — Hairlines inside the sidebar. *Use for:* Dividers between nav sections, and the sidebar's own trailing edge.
    - **Not** `border`, which is tuned against page surfaces.
- **`sidebar-ring`** — Focus indicator inside the sidebar. *Use for:* `focus-visible` on nav items.
    - **Not** `ring`, which is tuned against page surfaces.

### typography (25)

- **`display-4xl`** — The largest type: display-lg through display-4xl. Marketing-scale, one per view at most. *Use for:* A landing page hero, a section opener on a brand surface.
    - **Not** `heading-1` for page titles. Display is a *statement*; headings are *structure*. A settings page titled in display-3xl looks like an advert.
- **`display-3xl`** — The largest type: display-lg through display-4xl. Marketing-scale, one per view at most. *Use for:* A landing page hero, a section opener on a brand surface.
    - **Not** `heading-1` for page titles. Display is a *statement*; headings are *structure*. A settings page titled in display-3xl looks like an advert.
- **`display-2xl`** — The largest type: display-lg through display-4xl. Marketing-scale, one per view at most. *Use for:* A landing page hero, a section opener on a brand surface.
    - **Not** `heading-1` for page titles. Display is a *statement*; headings are *structure*. A settings page titled in display-3xl looks like an advert.
- **`display-xl`** — The largest type: display-lg through display-4xl. Marketing-scale, one per view at most. *Use for:* A landing page hero, a section opener on a brand surface.
    - **Not** `heading-1` for page titles. Display is a *statement*; headings are *structure*. A settings page titled in display-3xl looks like an advert.
- **`display-lg`** — The largest type: display-lg through display-4xl. Marketing-scale, one per view at most. *Use for:* A landing page hero, a section opener on a brand surface.
    - **Not** `heading-1` for page titles. Display is a *statement*; headings are *structure*. A settings page titled in display-3xl looks like an advert.
- **`heading-1`** — Structural document headings, heading-1 through heading-4. *Use for:* The real outline of a page. Pick the level by depth in the document, not by desired size.
    - **Not** `display` for size, or `title` for structure. If it belongs in a table of contents, it is a heading.
- **`heading-2`** — Structural document headings, heading-1 through heading-4. *Use for:* The real outline of a page. Pick the level by depth in the document, not by desired size.
    - **Not** `display` for size, or `title` for structure. If it belongs in a table of contents, it is a heading.
- **`heading-3`** — Structural document headings, heading-1 through heading-4. *Use for:* The real outline of a page. Pick the level by depth in the document, not by desired size.
    - **Not** `display` for size, or `title` for structure. If it belongs in a table of contents, it is a heading.
- **`heading-4`** — Structural document headings, heading-1 through heading-4. *Use for:* The real outline of a page. Pick the level by depth in the document, not by desired size.
    - **Not** `display` for size, or `title` for structure. If it belongs in a table of contents, it is a heading.
- **`title-lg`** — The title of a *component*, not of a document. *Use for:* A card's heading, a dialog title, a section label inside a panel.
    - **Not** `heading-*`. A card title is not part of the page outline, and using a heading tier for it produces a document structure that lies to a screen reader's heading navigation.
- **`title-sm`** — The title of a *component*, not of a document. *Use for:* A card's heading, a dialog title, a section label inside a panel.
    - **Not** `heading-*`. A card title is not part of the page outline, and using a heading tier for it produces a document structure that lies to a screen reader's heading navigation.
- **`body-lg`** — The reading tier: body-lg through body-xs. Prose and long-form content. *Use for:* Paragraphs, descriptions, help text, anything a person reads a sentence of.
    - **Not** `label-*`. Body is for reading, label is for naming. A form's help text is body; the field's name is a label. Getting this wrong is why some UIs feel like a wall of controls.
- **`body-md`** — The reading tier: body-lg through body-xs. Prose and long-form content. *Use for:* Paragraphs, descriptions, help text, anything a person reads a sentence of.
    - **Not** `label-*`. Body is for reading, label is for naming. A form's help text is body; the field's name is a label. Getting this wrong is why some UIs feel like a wall of controls.
- **`body-sm`** — The reading tier: body-lg through body-xs. Prose and long-form content. *Use for:* Paragraphs, descriptions, help text, anything a person reads a sentence of.
    - **Not** `label-*`. Body is for reading, label is for naming. A form's help text is body; the field's name is a label. Getting this wrong is why some UIs feel like a wall of controls.
- **`body-xs`** — The reading tier: body-lg through body-xs. Prose and long-form content. *Use for:* Paragraphs, descriptions, help text, anything a person reads a sentence of.
    - **Not** `label-*`. Body is for reading, label is for naming. A form's help text is body; the field's name is a label. Getting this wrong is why some UIs feel like a wall of controls.
- **`label-lg`** — The naming tier: label-lg through label-xs. Short, denser, slightly heavier. *Use for:* Field labels, table column headers, button text, tab titles, chip text.
    - **Not** `body-*` at the same size. Labels carry more weight and tighter leading because they are scanned, not read.
- **`label-md`** — The naming tier: label-lg through label-xs. Short, denser, slightly heavier. *Use for:* Field labels, table column headers, button text, tab titles, chip text.
    - **Not** `body-*` at the same size. Labels carry more weight and tighter leading because they are scanned, not read.
- **`label-sm`** — The naming tier: label-lg through label-xs. Short, denser, slightly heavier. *Use for:* Field labels, table column headers, button text, tab titles, chip text.
    - **Not** `body-*` at the same size. Labels carry more weight and tighter leading because they are scanned, not read.
- **`label-xs`** — The naming tier: label-lg through label-xs. Short, denser, slightly heavier. *Use for:* Field labels, table column headers, button text, tab titles, chip text.
    - **Not** `body-*` at the same size. Labels carry more weight and tighter leading because they are scanned, not read.
- **`caption`** — The smallest page-register tier. Metadata beneath something. *Use for:* Image captions, timestamps, footnotes, a card's secondary line.
    - **Not** `text-overline`. Caption sits *below* and explains; overline sits *above* and categorises.
- **`mono-xl`** — The monospace family: mono-xl through mono-sm, plus mono-caption. *Use for:* Code, identifiers, hashes, keyboard keys, and any figure where digits must align in a column.
    - **Not** the sans tiers for numeric data. Proportional digits make a column of numbers ragged; that is what `text-ui-num` solves in chrome and mono solves on a page.
- **`mono-lg`** — The monospace family: mono-xl through mono-sm, plus mono-caption. *Use for:* Code, identifiers, hashes, keyboard keys, and any figure where digits must align in a column.
    - **Not** the sans tiers for numeric data. Proportional digits make a column of numbers ragged; that is what `text-ui-num` solves in chrome and mono solves on a page.
- **`mono-md`** — The monospace family: mono-xl through mono-sm, plus mono-caption. *Use for:* Code, identifiers, hashes, keyboard keys, and any figure where digits must align in a column.
    - **Not** the sans tiers for numeric data. Proportional digits make a column of numbers ragged; that is what `text-ui-num` solves in chrome and mono solves on a page.
- **`mono-caption`** — The monospace family: mono-xl through mono-sm, plus mono-caption. *Use for:* Code, identifiers, hashes, keyboard keys, and any figure where digits must align in a column.
    - **Not** the sans tiers for numeric data. Proportional digits make a column of numbers ragged; that is what `text-ui-num` solves in chrome and mono solves on a page.
- **`mono-sm`** — The monospace family: mono-xl through mono-sm, plus mono-caption. *Use for:* Code, identifiers, hashes, keyboard keys, and any figure where digits must align in a column.
    - **Not** the sans tiers for numeric data. Proportional digits make a column of numbers ragged; that is what `text-ui-num` solves in chrome and mono solves on a page.

### radii (7)

- **`none`** — Square. A deliberate 0. *Use for:* Edge-to-edge surfaces, table cells, anything whose corners meet another element's corners.
    - **Not** omitting a radius class. Stating `none` records the intent; omitting it means the next person cannot tell square-on-purpose from square-by-accident.
- **`xs`** — The tightest real corner. Reads as 'crisp', not 'rounded'. *Use for:* Tool-chrome controls, tree rows, small swatches — anywhere the radius should be felt but not seen. The workspace register runs ~5px on essentially everything.
    - **Not** `sm`. In a 24px-tall control an `sm` radius starts to read as a lozenge.
- **`sm`** — The default control corner. *Use for:* Inputs, buttons in the page register, badges, small cards.
- **`md`** — A container corner. *Use for:* Cards, panels, popovers, menus — surfaces that hold other things.
    - **Not** `sm`. A container should be softer than the controls inside it, or the nesting reads inverted.
- **`lg`** — A prominent container corner. *Use for:* Dialogs, sheets, hero media, feature cards.
- **`xl`** — The softest rectangular corner. A styling statement. *Use for:* Marketing surfaces, large imagery, a theme that wants a soft character.
    - **Not** `full`. `xl` is still a rectangle with soft corners; `full` is a capsule. Using `xl` on a small element makes it look like a failed capsule.
- **`full`** — A capsule or circle — radius exceeds half the height. *Use for:* Avatars, status dots, notification badges, pills, and page-register actions (the 'round action in a tight container' contrast that says *this is a control*).
    - **Not** any fixed radius, for circles. And NOT in tool chrome: neither Figma nor Paper has a single pill in its chrome, which is why the compact density scope flattens `--button-radius` to ~5px.

### layout (11)

- **`rhythm-unit`** — The vertical rhythm base — two spacing steps (8px at the default scale). Every vertical measure is a multiple of it, and it follows the density control with the spacing scale. *Use for:* Through `Stack`/`Row`/`Grid` gap numbers, which are rhythm units rather than pixels. A gap of 2 is 16px at the default scale, and grows or tightens with density.
    - **Not** arbitrary vertical spacing. The rhythm is what makes unrelated sections of a page feel like one document.
- **`grid-columns`** — The column count of the content grid — 12. *Use for:* `Grid`/`Columns`, WITHIN a region, for genuinely multi-column content.
    - **Not** using a column span as the page's reading width. A span is not a measure — see `measure-prose`.
- **`grid-gutter`** — The gap between grid columns. *Use for:* `Grid`/`Columns` spacing.
- **`page-inset`** — The page's outer breathing room, left and right. *Use for:* The gutter between content and the viewport edge, at every breakpoint.
    - **Not** a global max-width. Sable caps width per REGION by role, never once for the whole page.
- **`measure-prose`** — The maximum comfortable line length for prose, in `ch`. *Use for:* Any long-form text column.
    - **Not** a layout width. Measure and width are different things: a wide region can still hold a narrow measure, and capping the region instead makes everything else in it too narrow.
- **`region-form`** — The region cap for a form — narrow, because fields should not run long. *Use for:* Settings pages, auth screens, any column of inputs.
    - **Not** `region-content`. A 700px-wide text input is harder to use, not more generous.
- **`region-feed`** — The region cap for a scrolling list of items. *Use for:* Feeds, timelines, search results.
- **`region-content`** — The default region cap for mixed page content. *Use for:* Article bodies with media, documentation, most product pages.
- **`region-wide`** — A wide region for dense or tabular content. *Use for:* Data tables, dashboards, galleries — content that genuinely needs the room.
- **`region-full`** — No cap. Edge to edge. *Use for:* Hero imagery, full-bleed sections, and a workspace, which is always edge-to-edge.
- **`region-ultrawide (legacy — prefer region-full)`** — Deprecated. Kept so existing usage keeps resolving. *Use for:* Nothing new. Use `region-full`.
    - **Not** `region-full`, which is what this became.

### derived (10)

- **`canvas`** — The WORK surface — the artboard, the document being edited. *Use for:* Behind the thing the tool operates on. `WorkspaceCanvas` uses it.
    - **Not** `background`. The thing being edited is not the page behind the UI, and collapsing the two makes the document indistinguishable from its chrome.
- **`canvas-foreground`** — Ink paired with `canvas`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `canvas`. Use them as a pair — `bg-canvas text-canvas-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`panel`** — Docked chrome: the surface of a side panel or an inspector. *Use for:* `Panel`, `WorkspaceBar`, `StatusBar` backgrounds.
    - **Not** `card`. Panels are chrome and sit in a deliberately compressed tonal band — see DESIGN.md → Registers. A card's elevation language is wrong here.
- **`panel-foreground`** — Ink paired with `panel`. Evaluate the rendered contrast together; never choose it independently. *Use for:* Whenever the background is `panel`. Use them as a pair — `bg-panel text-panel-foreground` — so a theme can retune the surface and the ink together.
    - **Not** `foreground`. That is the ink for `background` only; on any other surface it is a contrast gamble that happens to pass in the default theme and fails in another.
- **`panel-raised`** — One step up from `panel`: a selected row, a hover fill, a nested well. *Use for:* Tree row selection, hovered panel rows, and the light square of a checkerboard.
    - **Not** `accent`. In a workspace the tonal band is only a few units wide; `accent` is a page-register step and reads as a shout in chrome.
- **`panel-field`** — The inset fill of a compact control docked in a panel. *Use for:* The `size="xs"` field rung (Input, SelectTrigger, ScrubField share it) and `<Button variant="field">`. A panel control of your own that should sit among those fields.
    - **Not** `canvas`. `canvas` names the work surface, and its step off the panel is too faint to read as a field in dark mode. This one is mixed from the panel itself, so it follows a theme that retunes the panel. Tune it with `--theme-panel-field`.
- **`panel-field-hover`** — The hover step of a `panel-field` control. *Use for:* `hover:bg-panel-field-hover` on anything filled with `panel-field`.
    - **Not** `hover:bg-panel-raised`. A fixed surface token as a hover is what the surface-hover lint rejects; this one is defined against the panel field it steps from.
- **`hairline`** — The 1px structural line that carries all separation in tool chrome. *Use for:* Between panel sections, under a toolbar, above a status bar.
    - **Not** a bigger tonal step. This is one of the two rules the workspace register deliberately reverses: on a page prefer space or tone over a line, in chrome the hairline *is* the structure.
- **`hairline-strong`** — A hairline that must be seen — an input edge, a swatch ring. *Use for:* Bounding a control whose fill is arbitrary (a colour swatch) or user content.
    - **Not** `hairline`, when the line would otherwise disappear against what it bounds.
- **`border-floating`** — The edge of a floating surface. Fainter than `border`: the shadow carries the elevation. *Use for:* Every floating surface — popover, menu, select, tooltip, dialog, sheet, toast, a floating panel — as `border-border-floating` or `ring-border-floating`, together with `bg-popover` and a `shadow-md`+ shadow. Derived for every theme (a faint alpha of the foreground); a theme may tune it with `--theme-border-floating`.
    - **Not** `border`. A full hairline plus a shadow stacks into a heavy outline around anything that floats. `border` is for resting edges: inputs, cards, badges.
